_comment: Where a pivotal-history scout looks, and the licence class each source's TEXT carries for a paid book (history/sourcing.md §5: pd | cc-by | facts-only | clue-only). The class goes on each fetched source's record (`fetch.py --license`); this list is the default, and a specific item overrides it when its own page says otherwise. When in doubt: facts-only. `basis` says why; `verify` is true where the class depends on the item and must be checked before the source is cited. A translation's date decides its licence, never the original's. Pictures follow history/sourcing.md §8 per file. The test suite checks every entry has a licence from the classes above.

sources.name: Wikipedia
sources.basis: CC BY-SA 4.0. Reusing its prose would put our text under share-alike: take the fact, never the passage. An encyclopedia for tier counting.
sources.use: Leads, dates, names, and the references at the foot of each article, which are the real sources to fetch.

sources.name: Wikisource
sources.basis: Hosts mostly public-domain texts, including old translations; each text page states its licence.
sources.use: Pre-1930 translations of ancient and medieval sources; the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica.

sources.name: Project Gutenberg
sources.basis: Public-domain texts in the United States. Strip the Gutenberg header and footer, which are not the work.
sources.use: Old translations (Caesar, Polybius, Livy, Plutarch, Arrian), memoirs and histories published before 1930.

sources.name: Internet Archive
sources.basis: Per item. A book published in the United States before 1930 is public domain there; anything later, or lending-only, is facts-only.
sources.use: Scanned books and their _djvu.txt OCR (history/sourcing.md §7 has the search recipes).

sources.name: Perseus Digital Library (Tufts)
sources.basis: The site's markup is CC BY-SA; most of its English translations are pre-1930 and public domain as texts. The translation's date decides.
sources.use: Greek and Latin historians in English, with section numbers.

sources.name: LacusCurtius (penelope.uchicago.edu)
sources.basis: Transcriptions of public-domain editions (older Loeb translations among them); each page names its edition and date.
sources.use: Cassius Dio, Plutarch, Polybius, Frontinus, Vegetius; Roman topography.

sources.name: Library of Congress (Chronicling America, maps, prints)
sources.basis: Newspapers before 1930 are public domain; other items state their rights.
sources.use: Contemporary reporting of 19th- and early 20th-century episodes; period maps.

sources.name: U.S. Army Center of Military History
sources.basis: Works of the U.S. federal government are not subject to copyright (17 U.S.C. §105). Images credited to others are not.
sources.use: The official histories ('green books'), campaign brochures, staff studies.

sources.name: Naval History and Heritage Command
sources.basis: U.S. federal government works (17 U.S.C. §105). Images credited to others are not.
sources.use: Action reports, combat narratives, oral histories, ship histories (DANFS).

sources.name: NSA Center for Cryptologic History
sources.basis: U.S. federal government works (17 U.S.C. §105).
sources.use: Declassified histories of codebreaking and signals intelligence.

sources.name: Air Force Historical Support Division / AFHRA
sources.basis: U.S. federal government works (17 U.S.C. §105).
sources.use: Airlift, air campaign and technology histories.

sources.name: U.S. National Archives
sources.basis: Federal records are public domain; donated materials may not be.
sources.use: Dispatches, logs, photographs, maps.

sources.name: Official Records of the Union and Confederate Armies and Navies
sources.basis: Published by the U.S. government, 1880–1927.
sources.use: Civil War reports in the commanders' own words.

sources.name: HyperWar (ibiblio)
sources.basis: Transcriptions of U.S. government histories and reports; a transcription adds no copyright. Cite the original work, with HyperWar as where it was read.
sources.use: Second World War official histories and action reports.

sources.name: UK National Archives and other Crown copyright material under the Open Government Licence
sources.basis: The Open Government Licence v3 allows reuse with attribution, like CC BY. Older Crown works whose copyright has expired are public domain; material not under the OGL is facts-only.
sources.use: Despatches, the London Gazette, official histories.

sources.name: Smithsonian Open Access
sources.basis: Items released as CC0.
sources.use: Objects, weapons, aircraft, ships, with their descriptions.

sources.name: The Avalon Project (Yale Law School)
sources.basis: Documents of law and diplomacy, mostly public-domain texts; each states its source edition.
sources.use: Treaties, terms of surrender, declarations.

sources.name: Internet History Sourcebooks (Fordham)
sources.basis: Mixed: many texts are public-domain translations, some are copyrighted and posted for teaching. Each text names its edition; a pre-1930 one may be reclassified pd for that item.
sources.use: Medieval chronicles in translation, and the editions to look for elsewhere.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (current)
sources.basis: Copyrighted. The 1911 edition, on Wikisource, is public domain.
sources.use: Confirming facts; leads.

sources.name: World History Encyclopedia
sources.basis: Articles are mostly under a non-commercial licence, which a paid book cannot reuse.
sources.use: Leads only; fetch the sources its articles cite.

sources.name: Livius.org
sources.basis: Copyrighted articles by named authors; its translations of ancient texts carry their own terms.
sources.use: Leads, chronology, and pointers to the ancient sources.

sources.name: Open-access scholarship (journals, university presses)
sources.basis: Per item. Many open-access works are CC BY-NC or CC BY-NC-ND, which a paid book cannot reuse; a CC BY item may be reclassified cc-by.
sources.use: Modern estimates of numbers, archaeology, logistics studies.

sources.name: Enthusiast and war-gaming sites, forums, video, AI summaries
sources.basis: history/sourcing.md §2: clues tell you what to look for and never count.
sources.use: Finding names and dates to chase in a citable source.
